title: SuccessConnect 2026: Joule Agents Are Here. Is Your SAP SuccessFactors Architecture Ready?
author: nageshpolu
text:
My firsthand view from Las Vegas: the breakthroughs, the real availability status, and the technical questions that matter after the keynote. 

 Three days at SuccessConnect in Las Vegas convinced me of one thing: the next test for SAP SuccessFactors is not whether AI can answer an HR question. It is whether an agent can take the right action, in the right system, with the right permission, and leave enough evidence for us to trust the result. 
 I was in the audience when Siva Sundaresan walked through the expanding Joule Assistant portfolio. On the screen was a dense slide labelled “Available this month.” Another was labelled “Coming soon.” I photographed both. 

 They looked like product-roadmap slides. To me, they looked like an architecture review waiting to happen. 
 Configuration Transport Agent. Role-Based Permissions Agent. HCM Audit Agent. Skills Governance Agent. Payroll Alert Resolution Agent. Winston recruiting capabilities. Onboarding Task Management. 
 Each name suggests a task an HR technology team knows well. Each also raises a less glamorous question: what happens when the agent needs to change something? 
 At SAP Connect 2026, Christian Klein connected the Autonomous Enterprise vision across business functions. In the SuccessFactors keynote, Siva brought that ambition into Plan, Hire, Manage, Pay, Develop, and Grow . 

 I spent time with Joule Studio and followed the demonstrations and roadmap discussions. The announcements were substantial. But the most important takeaway from my three days was not a count of agents. 
 My thesis: agentic HCM shifts complexity from navigating screens to governing decisions and actions across systems. 
 That is where the real customer value and the real implementation risk now sit. 
 1. The breakthrough isn't a better chatbot. It's a different unit of work. 
 We have spent years building HR landscapes around transactions: create a position, approve a requisition, update a job record, assign learning, investigate an exception. 
 Each transaction has its place in a process, usually with handoffs between teams and applications. 
 Autonomous HCM starts from a different question: what outcome is the business trying to achieve? 
 Siva described three connected pillars: 
 Automate: Reduce repetitive work. 
 Redesign: Change how people and AI perform work together. 
 Reinvent: Rethink how organizations recruit, develop, move, and reward their workforce. 
 SAP also discussed 20 outcome-oriented opportunities across the employee lifecycle. 
 Those are important distinctions. Automating a weak process does not make it a good process. 
 Take a business request for ten additional specialists. 
 Today's response may be ten requisitions. Tomorrow's better question might be whether the business needs ten hires, some redeployment, targeted learning, contingent capacity, or a redesign of the underlying work. 
 That requires organizational data, financial context, skills evidence, and an understanding of what the business actually does. 
 For an HR architect, the difference is profound. 
 A system can execute a well-defined transaction. An outcome often crosses several systems of record. 
 We are not removing the integration problem. We are moving it behind a simpler experience. 
 2. Three agents I would put through a real customer test 
 I am deliberately starting with technical administration, not the flashiest employee demo. 
 These are scenarios in which an incorrect action can be expensive, even when the conversation looks convincing. 
 Test A: Configuration Transport Agent. Can it move a change without losing control? 
 In a typical DEV-QAS-PROD landscape, a successful transport depends on more than selecting an object and clicking Import. 
 We need to know what changed, what depends on it, whether the target is ready, and how the business process will be tested afterward. 
 SAP's learning documentation describes an agent that can: 
 Search configuration changes by date, modifier, and area. 
 Create or update transport bundles. 
 Initiate transport and request validation. 
 Guide an administrator through import. 
 Present validation findings, including warnings and errors. 
 For a selected bundle, SAP describes checks around validation status, dependencies, and maintenance-window considerations before import. 
 Search results that require asynchronous reporting include a freshness indicator and are retained for 24 hours. 
 That is considerably more useful than a chatbot that merely explains Configuration Transport Center. 
 My acceptance test: Modify a controlled Employee Central or platform configuration in DEV. Ask the agent to locate the change, create a bundle, review what it included, move it to QAS, and inspect validation warnings. 
 Then confirm the outcome against the native transport record and execute the actual business-process regression test. 
 What would make me reject the result? 
 A bundle that silently picks up unrelated changes, an unexplained dependency warning, missing authorization boundaries, or a success message that is mistaken for end-to-end functional validation. 
 Availability check: SAP Learning currently labels the HR System Assistant and Configuration Transport Agent as Early Adopter Care (EAC) . The “Available this month” keynote slide should not be interpreted as universal tenant availability. 
 Test B: Role-Based Permissions Agent. Does it solve the right access problem? 
 Consider a manager who cannot access an organizational feature. 
 In RBP, the answer can involve a permission, role, permission group, role assignment, and target population. 
 Granting broader access can make the immediate complaint disappear while introducing a security problem. 
 SAP documents an agent that can investigate why a user lacks access, list roles and permissions, identify who has a specific permission, and propose a fix with reasoning and impact information. 
 In a supported case, it can add a user to a static permission group after confirmation. 
 It is also currently in EAC. 
 My acceptance test: Reproduce a known access issue with a test user. Ask for the diagnosis, compare the explanation with the actual role-assignment chain, and inspect the scope of the proposed fix before approving any change. 
 One question matters more than how quickly the agent responds: 
 Did it restore the intended access without granting more than the user needs? 
 Test C: HCM Audit Agent. Can it show the evidence, not merely an answer? 
 Imagine a sensitive employee field changed unexpectedly. 
 A support analyst may need Change Audit, Read Audit, login activity, and proxy-session context to understand what happened. 
 SAP describes the HCM Audit Agent correlating Change, Read, and General Audit sources to investigate data changes, permissions, access to sensitive information, login events, and proxy activity. 
 This is potentially valuable because the investigation crosses evidence sources that an administrator would otherwise examine separately. 
 There is a fundamental boundary: 
 The agent can report only what the underlying audit logs captured. 
 It does not manufacture missing evidence. It is also documented as EAC. 
 My acceptance test: Perform a controlled change and a permitted read of test data. Establish the expected audit records first, then ask the agent to reconstruct the event timeline. 
 Evaluate source traceability, omissions, timestamps, and access restrictions, not just the quality of its narrative. 
 Across these three tests, I would measure four things: accuracy, time saved, permission discipline, and the ability to reconstruct what the agent did. 
 That is a much stronger business case than “we enabled three agents.” 
 3. Recruiting makes the architecture problem impossible to ignore 
 SmartRecruiters and SuccessFactors offer a useful way to think about end-to-end agentic work because the process naturally crosses application boundaries. 
 Consider this illustrative implementation scenario , not a claim about a particular keynote demo: 
 A position is approved in SAP SuccessFactors Employee Central. 
 A recruiting requisition is created and managed in SmartRecruiters. 
 Winston capabilities assist the recruiting team with supported matching, screening, interview, or knowledge activities. 
 After the hiring decision and required approvals, the supported handoff initiates the next hiring and onboarding steps. 
 Downstream systems receive the appropriate worker information at the correct point in the lifecycle. 
 On paper, it is one hiring outcome. 
 Technically, it contains multiple records, owners, statuses, identities, and failure modes. 
 If the position changes after requisition creation, which information can be updated, and where? 
 If the offer is withdrawn after a downstream event is triggered, what is the reversal or correction path? 
 If a candidate is a rehire, which matching and person-identity rules determine the right employee record? 
 If an event is retried, how do we avoid duplicates? 
 These are ordinary integration design questions. Agents do not remove them. 
 In some cases, they make them more urgent because users may perceive the experience as a single continuous workflow. 
 SAP's October SmartRecruiters implementation guidance is a useful reminder: SmartRecruiters can be deployed without Employee Central, but that changes the availability of productized master-data synchronization, position-led hiring, and standard hire handoff. 
 An agent-enabled experience cannot be assumed to erase those product boundaries. 
 The recruiting portfolio shown at SuccessConnect included Winston Companion, Interview, Chat, Match, and other capabilities. 
 But an assistant name is not an integration specification. 
 Before committing to a design, customers still need to verify the supported actions, APIs, ownership of each object, the required identity model, and the lifecycle events actually delivered by the product. 
 This is also why I separate candidate-facing experiences from employee- or recruiter-facing Joule experiences. 
 Authentication, privacy, and permitted actions differ by audience. 
 4. TechWolf changes the workforce conversation, but not overnight 
 One of the biggest announcements came as Day 2 began: SAP had entered into an agreement to acquire TechWolf. 
 For me, this was not simply another AI acquisition headline. 
 It addresses a problem I see at the intersection of workforce planning and Talent Intelligence Hub: 
 Organizations often know which jobs exist, but not enough about the work people actually perform. 
 TechWolf's Context Graph for Work is designed to build a continuously updated view of tasks, applied skills, and labor-market context using connected business and HR data. 
 That could improve the evidence behind decisions on hiring, internal mobility, reskilling, and role redesign. 
 Now connect that direction with SAP's announced Workforce Planning Assistant. 
 SAP plans for it to combine SuccessFactors workforce data, SAP Fieldglass contingent-labor information, and SAP Cloud ERP financial information through SAP Enterprise Planning. 
 The ambition is to recommend a more effective mix of hiring, redeployment, reskilling, and external talent. 
 Here is the non-obvious implication: 
 An organization may have to improve its job architecture before its workforce intelligence becomes useful. 
 A poor role taxonomy or inconsistent skills definitions cannot be repaired merely by presenting the information through Joule. 
 SAP's Job Architecture Maintenance Agent makes that dependency concrete. 
 Its published learning material describes comparing Job Profile Builder role definitions with skills from Growth Portfolio and job requisitions, identifying missing role-skill mappings and orphaned roles, and proposing updates for administrator confirmation. 
 Job Profile Builder and Talent Intelligence Hub are stated prerequisites.

title: SAP’s Competency Framework Is Now AI-Ready, Are You?
author: VRobinson
text:
Our customers have always turned to SAP partners who know their industries, understand their businesses, and provide them with the tools they need for business success. Today, SAP customers are looking for tools that leverage AI for operational efficiency and a competitive edge. IDC reports that AI spending will see 53% year-over-year growth to reach $700 billion by 2029 globally. However, that same research found that about half of those use cases will miss their ROI targets due to “unclear business gains, weak human-to-machine collaboration, and poor data foundations.” These AI implementation challenges and uncertainty will drive enterprises to find the expertise they need – and SAP wants to ensure partners are prepared to meet this growing demand. 
 To ensure partners are AI-ready in the age of the Autonomous Enterprise, SAP is adjusting its Competency Framework for 2027. As announced in June 2026 , SAP renamed the SAP Business Technology Platform (SAP BTP) competency as the SAP Business AI Platform competency. But SAP did more than change the name. SAP took a holistic look at the framework to ensure partner AI readiness is recognized and rewarded across the board. With this updated competency, partners can show their customers and prospects that they are prepared and skilled with various AI implementations, and the Competency Framework helps promote that AI-expertise to their markets. 

 Start with the Foundation: SAP Business AI Platform 
 The updated SAP Business AI Platform competency carries significant strategic meaning. It’s the first step in building a modernized Competency Framework that fully aligns with how partners and customers leverage SAP’s platform today with artificial intelligence at the center. As SAP’s portfolio evolves to make AI central to every solution, the Competency Framework will reflect that evolution — starting with the SAP Business AI platform. 
 Beginning in 2027, the competency evolves from its SAP BTP roots into four specializations that reflect SAP’s converged AI and data platform strategy : Technology Foundation, SAP Integration Suite, Artificial Intelligence, and SAP Business Data Cloud. 

 The Technology Foundation Specialization: Instill AI Literacy Across All LOBs 
 With the SAP Business AI Platform now established as the foundation of the AI-centric Competency Framework, it raises an important question: How do partners actually demonstrate they’re ready to deliver on SAP’s AI-first vision? The answer is the Technology Foundation specialization. 
 To achieve Advanced or Expert tier in SAP Cloud ERP, Supply Chain Management, Human Capital Management, Spend Management, or Customer Relationship Management, partners must hold the Technology Foundation specialization. That translates to partners who achieve those tiers not only have specializations in their solution areas but are also equipped to develop and implement AI agents. With every line-of-business (LOB) competency now including an AI component built into Advanced and Expert tiers, partners who reach these levels can help customers achieve the return they anticipate for their AI implementation projects while they differentiate their practices and grow their businesses. This reflects SAP's commitment to enabling partners to build and implement AI-powered, partner-led agents. The Technology Foundation specialization is the core building block of the SAP Business AI Platform and equips partners with the skills to lead in this space. 
 Also note that rather than requiring the Technology Foundation specialization in full, the SAP Cloud ERP Private competency introduces individual role requirements — Generative AI Developer and Data Architect — drawn directly from the Technology Foundation. This reflects the strategic importance of SAP Cloud ERP Private and ensures partners can deliver AI-enabled, data-driven implementations at the customer level. 
 Additionally, to help partners who have achieved their competencies under the previous requirements, SAP has expanded the safeguarding period from 90 to 180 days . This gives partners ample opportunity to learn and develop AI skills and expertise, while maintaining their current competency designation. 

 SAP Partner Finder: Your Direct Line to Customers 
 Earning competency is only half the story for SAP partners. The other half is making sure customers can see it. That's where SAP Partner Finder comes in. SAP Partner Finder is where prospects and existing customers go to find a reliable, skillful partner with proven understanding of their business and industry. In a market where customers are seeking AI expertise, an SAP Partner Finder profile is often the first impression — and the clearest signal of what an SAP partner brings to the table. This is one of the most important reasons that achieving the SAP Business AI Platform competency matters to partners. Once they’ve earned the competency, it shows up directly in their SAP Partner Finder profiles, giving customers immediate, credible proof that they are not only a platform expert but also an SAP partner skilled and equipped in the age of AI . 
 Furthermore, with the Technology Foundation specialization now woven into the Advanced and Expert tiers of line-of-business competencies, SAP partners’ AI readiness is reflected across their entire solution portfolio. For example, a customer searching for a Supply Chain or HCM partner will find partners with solution expertise but can also see a partner equipped to build and implement AI agents in that domain. The visibility that SAP Partner Finder provides is what turns hard-earned expertise into real market differentiation, demand generation, and business growth. 

 Full-Circle: From Competency to Customer 
 At its heart, the Competency Framework exists to help partners better position their specific skills and experience for improved market visibility and to help customers choose the best-fit partner for their requirements based on solution focus, expertise, and maturity. The journey partners take to earn and grow competency is ultimately a journey toward valuable customer relationships, especially as the demand for AI expertise grows. 
 Visit SAP Partner Portal for more information on the Competency Framework and to access enablement materials. Begin preparing today for the changes to the framework that reflect SAP’s AI-centered strategy and review your SAP Partner Finder profile to ensure it’s fully up to date.

title: Terraform + SAP BTP Trial: Build an Integration Suite Lab from Scratch
author: subhojitSaha
text:
Have you ever created the same SAP BTP subaccount, assigned entitlements, subscribed to applications, and configured destinations again and again? Terraform helps us describe the desired platform setup in text files and reproduce it consistently. 
 In this beginner-friendly tutorial, we will create a new BTP subaccount , allocate the Integration Suite trial entitlement , subscribe to Integration Suite , grant initial and developer access, and create a dummy HTTP destination . We will also activate the Cloud Integration capability in the browser —a deliberate manual step that Terraform does not currently cover through this BTP provider.

title: eSocial - Nota Técnica S-1.3 Nº 07/2026 - Fase 1 Concluída
author: AndersonMarques
text:
Olá, pessoal, 
 Concluímos a Fase 1 das entregas referentes à Nota Técnica S-1.3 Nº 07/2026 do eSocial. É uma nota com bastante impacto, com mais duas fases previstas até o final do ano — mas vamos por partes: 
 O que representa essa entrega? 
 Com a Fase 1 concluída, o módulo HCM passa a: 
 Gerar o XML do evento S-2500 para incluir os novos grupos e campos de localização do trabalho (localTrabalho e subgrupos), nome social (nmSoc), cargo (nmCargo), nome da função de confiança/cargo comissionado (nmFuncao) e CBO para função de confiança (CBOFuncao). 
 Gerar o XML dos eventos S-2299, S-2399 e S-2420 para incluir o novo campo indCPFDesvinc nos cenários de alteração de CPF. 
 Gerar os eventos S-2200 e S-2205 com o campo infoCota de acordo com as novas regras. 
 Gerar o evento S-2205 com o grupo infoDeficiencia de acordo com as novas regras. 
 SAP Notes liberadas 
 Aplique as SAP Notes na seguinte sequência: 
 3831094 - Prerequisite objects for SAP Note 3808467 
 3808467 - eSocial - S-2500 - Transformation and converter updates for NT 07/2026 
 3806789 - Prerequisite Objects for SAP Note 3806883 
 3806883 - eSocial S-2299/S-2399 - New field indCPFDesvinc - Technical Note S-1.3 Nº 07/2026 
 3819661 - eSocial S-1.3 NT 07/2026 - S-2200/S-2205 - Disregard of infoCota field 
 Principais mudanças realizadas 
 Solução para o campo indCPFDesvinc (eventos S-2299 e S-2399): 
 Ao reenviar um evento S-2299 ou S-2399 com status Aguardando correção que contenha o erro 1856, o sistema passa a gerar o XML com o campo indCPFDesvinc preenchido com o valor 9 . 
 Exemplo: 
 Considerando o cenário descrito acima, ao reenviar o evento, o sistema gera o arquivo XML contendo o campo <indCPFDesvinc> com valor 9 : 
 < mudancaCPF > 
 < novoCPF > XXXXXXXXXXX </ novoCPF > 
 < indCPFDesvinc > 9 </ indCPFDesvinc > 
 </ mudancaCPF > 

 Importante: Se você gerar o evento novamente, a solução não funcionará, pois o status mudará para Pronto para envio . Para corrigir, siga os passos abaixo: 
 Reenvie o evento. É esperado que o governo o rejeite novamente. 
 Em seguida, reenvie o evento com o status Aguardando correção — a solução funcionará corretamente. 
 Próximas entregas 
 Esta é apenas a primeira de três fases planejadas para a Nota Técnica S-1.3 Nº 07/2026: 
 Fase 1 Concluída ✅ 
 Fase 2 16 de novembro de 2026 
 Fase 3 14 de dezembro de 2026 
 Para acompanhar o planejamento completo, acesse: Regulatory Change Manager 
 Próximos passos 
 Implemente as SAP Notes liberadas pela SAP o quanto antes para garantir a conformidade com a Nota Técnica S-1.3 Nº 07/2026. 
 Para mais informações e documentação completa sobre este tema, acesse a página dedicada no Workzone: 👉 eSocial - Nota Técnica S-1.3 Nº 07/2026 
 Gostou deste conteúdo? Deixe seu like, compartilhe com colegas e registre dúvidas, experiências ou sugestões nos comentários! Siga a tag HCM Payroll Brazil na SAP Community para se manter sempre atualizado. 
 Atenciosamente, 
 Anderson Marques

title: SAP Commerce Cloud - OCC API with Swagger and OAuth authorization code with PKCE
author: joris_quenee
text:
Introduction 
 Starting with JDK 21, SAP Commerce Cloud introduces a new OAuth flow for end-user authentication. By default, the Swagger interface does not expose a dedicated authentication screen to support this flow. This article provides a concise guide on how to authenticate as an end user directly within Swagger for OCC API testing purposes. 
 Activation 
 First you need to activate Swagger. 
 In local.properties springdoc.swagger-ui.enabled=true 
 In localextensions.xml <extension name='swaggerintegration' /> 

 OAuth Clients 
 As mentioned in this following KBA https://me.sap.com/notes/0003738186 , you need to create dedicated OAuth clients for swagger usage. 
 Execute this following Impex in HAC OAuthClientDetails;clientId[unique=true];resourceIds;scope;authorizedGrantTypes;authorities;clientSecret;registeredRedirectUri;public;requireProofKey
;swagger;;basic;refresh_token,authorization_code,client_credentials;ROLE_TRUSTED_CLIENT;secret;https://localhost:9002/occ/v2/swagger-ui/oauth2-redirect.html;false;true
;swagger_public;;basic;refresh_token,authorization_code;ROLE_TRUSTED_CLIENT;;https://localhost:9002/occ/v2/swagger-ui/oauth2-redirect.html;true;true 
 From BackOffice, ensure that you have end-user account activated (Login disable : false) 

 Login 
 From Swagger : https://localhost:9002/occ/v2/swagger-ui/index.html 
 Login your swagger client in PKCE mode: swagger / secret 

 Then you should be redirected to end-user login page. Enter your end-user credential. 

 After that, you should be redirected to Swagger interface and ready to test. 
 Testing 
 Now you can test OCC API by executing some requests within end-user authorisation. To check that you're correctly recognise, you can run this following query : customer profile. 

 Note that current is used as user id. True user id is retrieved by SAP Commerce through OAuth token. 
 Expected output <?xml version='1.0' encoding='UTF-8'?>
 <user>
 <name>Men</name>
 <uid>men@hybris.com</uid>
 <active>false</active>
 <customerId>9cd038f9-2f7b-46d4-9148-58afe9c8806f</customerId>
 <displayUid>men@hybris.com</displayUid>
 <firstName>Men</firstName>
 <lastName>
 </lastName>
 <selected>false</selected>
 </user>

title: Trying to Sync to Cloud ALM Based on Model State? Here's Why It Breaks and How to Fix It.
author: lilit_ghazaryan
text:
A customer came to us wanting to sync their approved processes to SAP Cloud ALM automatically. The setup made sense: once a model reaches the right state in SPM, the SPG workflow triggers the Cloud ALM action and the sync happens without anyone touching it. They built the workflow, added the gateway condition based on Model State, and it never routed correctly. The field picker showed "No matching fields found" and the condition did nothing. 
 Part of the SPG Hidden Gems series: short posts on features, patterns, and fixes that rarely make it into the main documentation but save real time once you know them.

title: Upgrade your SAP Service and Asset Manager for Windows 4.0 custom client to MDK for Windows SDK 4.1
author: Gabor-Seres
text:
This blog post provides a step-by-step guide on how to upgrade a custom SAP Service and Asset Manager (SSAM) for Windows 4.0 client from MDK for Windows SDK 4.0 to 4.1 , including rebuilding and packaging the updated Windows application. 
 MDK for Windows 4.1 is intended for customers who build and maintain their own Windows clients using the MDK SDK. It does not apply to the SAP Service and Asset Manager for Windows 4.0 application distributed through the Microsoft Store. The SSAM Windows 4.0 metadata remains unchanged and is supported by both MDK for Windows SDK 4.0 and 4.1.

title: S/4HANA Cloud Public - Impact Analysis in Engineering Change Management not returning BOM & Routing
text:
Hello SAP Community, 
 We are currently implementing Engineering Change Management (ECM) in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition and are configuring the Impact Analysis functionality. 
 We have maintained the following configuration: 
 SSCUI 107224 - Define Change Record Types 
 SSCUI 105882 - Define Impact Modeler Objects Configuration 
 Our objective is to use Impact Analysis from a Change Record and identify impacted objects such as: 
 Bills of Material (BOMs) 
 Routings 
 Related Change Records 
 To support this, we also created a custom object type ( Z01 ) for Production Routings. 
 Issue 
 When we execute Impact Analysis from a Change Record, the expected impacted objects are not returned. 
 Additionally, when attempting to create an Impact Analysis Rule, we receive the following error: 
 "Insert Rule is not possible as Model data is incomplete." 
 Questions 
 What is the functional difference between MATERIAL and PRODUCT object types in the Impact Modeler? 
 Which object type should be used to analyze impacts on manufacturing objects such as BOMs and Routings? 
 Are Impact Analysis Rules mandatory for the functionality to work? 
 What configuration is required to resolve the "Model data is incomplete" error? 
 Has anyone successfully configured Impact Analysis to identify impacted BOMs and Routings in S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition? 
 Any guidance, configuration examples, or screenshots would be greatly appreciated. 
 Thank you in advance for your help!

title: Not able to add new entries in "Assign Item Categories"
author: srinath_ck
text:

title: SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition: Profit Center derived in Ledger View (0L) is missing in Entry View
author: SimonWCA
text:
Hello SAP Community, 
 I am looking for advice on the correct approach for handling Profit Center values in the Entry View versus the Ledger View in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition. 
 System and business scenario 
 SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition 
 Company code:Z3 
 Leading ledger: 0L 
 Scenario: Supplier invoice posting 
 G/L accounts involved: vendor reconciliation account and expense account 
 Current behavior 
 When posting a supplier invoice, the Profit Center is automatically derived by SAP for the expense line. The derived Profit Center is visible in the Ledger View for ledger 0L . 
 However, in the Entry View, the Profit Center on the vendor reconciliation line is empty, even though the Profit Center is available in the Ledger View. 
 This causes a practical issue because applications that read the Entry View, such as Manage Supplier Line Items, do not show the Profit Center as expected. 
 What I have tested 
 I implemented the BAdI FIN_ACDOC_ITEM_SUBSTITUTION in the Custom Logic app. 
 When I assign a fixed Profit Center value to the vendor reconciliation line, the value is successfully saved and displayed in the Entry View after posting. 
 Therefore, the BAdI can populate the field. However, hardcoding a Profit Center is not a viable solution. I would like to use the Profit Center that SAP already derives automatically for the corresponding posting. 
 I also checked FIN_CODING_BLOCK_SUBSTITUTION . According to its documentation, Profit Center substitution is restricted to specific scenarios and does not appear to support this general supplier invoice use case. 
 Questions 
 Is it standard and expected behavior that the Profit Center derived for ledger 0L is not necessarily available in the Entry View? 
 Is there a supported way to transfer the Profit Center automatically derived for the expense line to the vendor reconciliation line in the Entry View? 
 Can the standard Profit Center derivation logic be reused within FIN_ACDOC_ITEM_SUBSTITUTION , or is the derived value only available later in the posting process? 
 Is there another supported BAdI, substitution rule, or configuration option for this scenario? 
 Alternatively, should the Entry View be left unchanged, even if this means that the Profit Center shown in the Ledger View is not displayed in applications that read the Entry View? Is there a recommended approach for reporting or operational processes in this case? 
 My goal is not to implement a separate Profit Center derivation rule . I would like the Entry View to reflect the Profit Center that SAP already derives automatically, wherever this is supported by the standard posting logic. 
 Any recommendations on the intended standard behavior and the supported solution would be greatly appreciated. 
 Thank you!

title: SAP Business ByDesign ABSL: Why Does the Same Logic Behave Differently in Different Scenarios?
author: Mohamd_Yasif_0001
text:
If you have worked with ABSL in SAP Business ByDesign for a while, you may have come across a situation where your script works as expected in one scenario but not in another. 
 You check the code, review the conditions, and everything looks correct. Yet, when the same process is triggered in a different way, the expected result doesn't happen. 
 Before changing the code, it is worth checking how the script is being executed. 
 In ByDesign, the result doesn't always depend on the logic inside the script. The business object, the event being triggered, the data available at that point, and the way the record is created or updated can all affect the outcome. 
 Let's look at a few situations that are worth checking when troubleshooting ABSL. 
 1. Is the script actually being triggered? 
 One of the first things I would check is whether the script is being executed at all. 
 For example, you might have written validation logic in a BeforeSave script. It works when a user creates or updates a record through the UI, but the same validation doesn't appear to work when the record is created through another process. 
 It is tempting to assume that something is wrong with the condition or the script itself. However, the first question should be whether that operation invokes the expected logic. 
 When investigating this, check the following: 

 How is the business object record being created or updated? 

 Is the expected event supported and triggered for that operation? 

 Does the script execute but skip the logic because of a condition? 

 Is the record being processed through a different business object or operation? 
 These checks help narrow down the issue before you start changing the code. 
 2. Check the data available when the script runs 
 Sometimes, the script executes correctly, but the values available during execution are different from what you expect. 
 Consider a simple condition that checks a document status before executing some business logic. 
 if (this.StatusCode == "InTransfer")
{
 // Execute business logic
} 
 The code inside the condition will run only if the status matches the expected value. 
 If the record has a different status when the script executes, the condition won't be satisfied. This can happen when the logic depends on a value that is populated or updated at another stage of the process. 
 When debugging, compare the actual field values in the scenario that works with those in the scenario that fails. 
 Pay particular attention to status fields, identifiers, associations, and fields that may not be populated immediately. 
 Also, make sure the example field and status code above match the actual business object and code values used in your implementation. 
 3. Why does it work for one record but not for multiple records? 
 Another situation worth considering is when processing a single record works correctly, but processing multiple records produces unexpected results. 
 There are several possible reasons for this. One record may contain different input values, a condition may be satisfied for one record but not another, or an external request may return different results. 
 Instead of immediately modifying the script, compare the records individually. 
 For each record, check whether the expected script executes, whether the conditions are satisfied, and whether the required values are assigned and saved. 
 If the script calls an external API, also verify the request and response for each record. A successful response for one record doesn't necessarily mean that all subsequent requests will return the same data. 
 This is why testing with multiple records is important whenever the business process supports it. 
 4. The API call succeeds, but the fields are still empty 
 When working with integrations, another common area to investigate is the gap between retrieving data and seeing that data in the business object. 
 An external request can succeed without guaranteeing that the expected values are stored correctly. 
 For example, the issue could be related to the response structure, how the response is parsed, the field assignment, or the subsequent save operation. 
 I would check the flow in this order: 

 Is the request being sent with the correct parameters? 

 Does the response contain the expected values? 

 Is the script reading the correct elements from the response? 

 Are those values being assigned to the intended fields? 

 Are the values persisted in the business object? 

 If the values are persisted, are the relevant UI fields correctly configured to display them? 
 Checking each stage separately makes it easier to identify where the problem actually occurs. 
 If the data is already saved but is not visible on the screen, there may be no need to change the integration logic at all. 
 5. A few things I check before changing ABSL code 
 When an ABSL script doesn't behave as expected, I find it useful to start with a few basic questions: 

 Is the correct business object and event involved? 

 Does the script execute in the scenario where the issue occurs? 

 Are the field values and conditions what I expect them to be at runtime? 

 Is any part of the logic dependent on another service or process? 

 Does the issue occur with every record or only specific records? 

 Are the values missing from the saved data, or are they simply not visible in the UI? 
 These questions may sound simple, but they help separate an execution issue from a logic issue or a data issue. 
 It is also worth reproducing the problem in a test environment before making changes to a working implementation. 
 Final thoughts 
 ABSL troubleshooting is not always about finding an error in the code. Sometimes, the more important part is understanding when the script runs, what data is available at that point, and how the business process reaches that stage. 
 When something works in one scenario but fails in another, I would start by comparing the execution paths rather than rewriting the logic straight away. 
 Understanding that difference can save a lot of debugging time, especially when working with custom business objects and integrations in SAP Business ByDesign. 
 Have you encountered similar behaviour with ABSL? It would be interesting to hear how other developers approach these situations, particularly when the same business logic is triggered through different processes.

title: SAP Strengthens the Foundation for the Autonomous Enterprise with SAP Cloud ERP Private 2025 FPS02
author: Maura Hameroff
text:
SAP Cloud ERP Private 2025 Feature Pack Stack 02 (FPS02) delivers new capabilities that help organizations move from AI experimentation toward intelligent, governed business execution faster. 

 The release combines AI agents that can work directly with core business processes and adds new regulatory compliance capabilities and industry-specific innovations across asset-intensive industries, retail, and energy sectors. Together, these enhancements help strengthen the foundation for organizations that need to scale AI responsibly. 

 Building the foundation for enterprise AI 
 Tune into the Rise into the Future webinar “AI That Works: From ERP Foundation to Autonomous Enterprise” on November 11 

 Register today 

 As organizations explore how AI can drive business outcomes, one challenge keeps surfacing: AI alone is not enough. To operate at enterprise scale, AI needs access to trusted data, process context, business rules, and governance. 

 This is why the conversation about AI increasingly becomes a conversation about ERP. AI agents require more than information. They need to understand what actions are permitted, which controls must be respected, and when decisions require human review. SAP Cloud ERP Private can provide this foundation through integrated business processes, harmonized data, and enterprise-grade governance. FPS02 helps extend these capabilities, bringing intelligence directly into the processes where business happens. 

 AI embedded within business processes 

 FPS02 introduces AI agents and AI-assisted capabilities across key business domains, helping organizations automate routine work while maintaining oversight and accountability. 

 In finance , agents and AI-assisted capabilities help support processes spanning planning and forecasting, period-close activities, working capital management, tax processes, and compliance operations. Rather than requiring employees to manually identify issues and coordinate follow-up activities, SAP Cloud ERP Private and analytical business insights can surface risks, recommend actions, and help manage exceptions. 

 In sales order-to-cash processes , agents enable sales teams to quickly identify fulfillment issues, receive resolutions, and create or update sales orders directly in their workflow, which helps minimize delays and improve customer satisfaction. 

 Joule and SAP Document AI help streamline quality management by uploading, extracting, and matching certificate data, flagging exceptions, and creating pre-filled defects from natural-language inputs and source documents to help accelerate review, accuracy, and inspection release. 

 By receiving key observations, recommendations, and a clear action plan directly within business processes, employees can focus on judgment and expertise rather than information gathering and exception management. 

 Compliance built into the core 

 FPS02 also delivers important regulatory capabilities directly within SAP Cloud ERP Private. 

 The release includes support for IFRS 18 indirect-method cash flow statement reporting, helping organizations prepare for evolving financial reporting requirements. Additional updates include support for Germany’s AUSWIB1M foreign-trade reporting requirements and Canada First Nations Tax determination with GST499-1 return generation. By incorporating these capabilities into standard business processes, organizations can address compliance obligations while maintaining consistent governance and operational efficiency. 

 Industry innovation across critical operations 

 FPS02 deepens industry-specific capabilities across asset-intensive operations, upstream oil and gas, defense and security, and retail. 

 For asset-intensive industries , enhancements further integrate permit-to-work processes into maintenance operations, helping ensure operational controls are embedded directly within workflows. Upstream oil and gas organizations can gain new capabilities that extend Joule into production and revenue accounting, while SAP Document AI helps interpret gas plant statements and propose accounting entries for review. Defense and security organizations can benefit from innovations supporting equipment allocation and ERP operations in limited-connectivity environments. 

 Retail organizations gain four new data products that help expose retail master data through SAP Business Data Cloud, working to create a stronger foundation for future AI-driven processes. FPS02 also introduces operational enhancements including support for partial order fulfillment scenarios, GS1 2D barcode enablement, and expanded product traceability through serial-number integration between point-of-sale and inventory processes. 

 Advancing the Autonomous Enterprise 

 The Autonomous Enterprise is not built through a single AI breakthrough or software release. It emerges through the combination of trusted business data, integrated processes, governance, and intelligent capabilities working together across the enterprise. 

 SAP Cloud ERP Private 2025 FPS02 helps advance that foundation in concrete terms: by embedding intelligence within business processes, strengthening compliance capabilities, and expanding industry-specific innovation. 

 To explore the full FPS02 release and its implications for your business, visit SAP Community . 

 Maura Hameroff is chief marketing officer for SAP Cloud ERP Private and RISE with SAP.

title: Industry AI: Deep Industry Knowledge, Forward-Deployed Engineering, Measurable Value
author: Dominik Metzger
text:
Enterprise AI has reached an inflection point. 
 SAP Connect in 2026: Advancing the Autonomous Enterprise 

 Read the innovation news guide 

 But while there is enormous excitement about what AI can do, we are still measuring progress the wrong way. The number of models, pilots, or agents a company deploys tells us very little. What matters is whether AI transforms the core processes where business value is actually created. 

 Can it steer demand fulfillment to high-margin business when supply is disrupted? Can it help release a pharmaceutical batch without compromising quality and compliance? Can it resolve a critical maintenance issue before it turns into an outage? 

 This is where enterprise AI becomes real and where generic intelligence reaches its limits. 

 From pharmaceutical supply chains and manufacturing quality management to asset maintenance, trading, and retail, the hardest industry problems are deeply contextual. They are shaped by decades of interconnected processes, strict regulations, and operational constraints. Solving them demands more than a powerful model. It requires trusted business data, integrated processes, rock-solid governance, and a deep industry domain expertise–the very foundation upon which we are building SAP’s Industry AI . At the same time it demands a team which is obsessed with customer problem solving and world-class forward deployed engineers. 

 This convergence of industry depth and forward deployed engineering (FDE) is where the next wave of enterprise value will be unlocked. 

 Start with the value, not the technology 

 AI innovation too often turns into a search for problems to solve. We take the opposite approach: start with the customer’s desired business value and work backward. 

 Where is margin leaking? Why is there lost sales? What operational decisions take too long? What production deferment can be prevented? 

 The goal is no longer just incremental productivity for individual users. It is moving toward autonomous operations. Across industries, organizations need to compress the cycle between detecting an issue, simulating options and impact, deciding the right response, executing corrective actions, and learning from outcomes–in a compounding loop. What once took days can increasingly happen in minutes. 

 Through our forward-deployed engineering model, we co-develop tailored capabilities alongside customers. We solve high-stakes challenges that have no off-the-shelf answers, then turn those proven solutions into scalable software capabilities for entire industries. This is not innovation from a distance. It is built with the people who live these challenges every day. 

 Autonomous operations make this possible. Within clearly defined business guardrails, AI agents identify disruptions, model scenarios, evaluate trade-offs, orchestrate execution, and improve via feedback loops–with human experts firmly in the loop and on-the-loop to validate critical decisions and steer strategic direction. 

 Co-innovation as a catalyst for impact 

 The most valuable AI solutions are never built in isolation. They are forged inside live operating environments. 

 Takeda Pharmaceuticals, a global leader in research-based biopharmaceuticals, is applying this thinking to its future operating model. 

 According to Rebecca Kaufmann, senior vice president and head of Enterprise Platforms a Takeda Pharmaceuticals , “AI represents the key enabler for Takeda’s transformation for the future. We are combining the SAP industry and technology knowledge with our organizational real-life experience. The supply chain planning assistant will provide us with AI-detected root causes and AI-suggested remediation and also automated performance tracking resulting in a self-healing capability.” 

 That ambition–shifting from passive detection to systems that continuously learn, recommend, and self-heal—is taking hold across sectors. 

 Doehler, a global producer of natural ingredients for the food, beverage, life sciences, and nutrition industries, is already demonstrating what this looks like on the factory and logistics floor. 

 “Our people’s greatest value lies in deciding what to do next, and now they can focus entirely on that,” said Stephan Schissler, co-chief information officer at Doehler GmbH. “The Logistics Issue Resolution Agent detects the root cause, recommends the resolution, and turns a multi-hour firefight into a one-click decision. Our logistics team has recovered roughly a third of the time once lost to troubleshooting, and our processes are becoming self-resolving rather than exception-driven.” 

 These examples reinforce a decisive rule: AI delivers maximum return when it eliminates operational drag, freeing professionals to focus on judgment, strategy, and business outcomes. 

 AI that thinks like the industry 

 As AI moves from passive recommendation to intelligent execution, industry context becomes paramount. 

 The question is no longer whether an AI agent can take an action. The question is whether it understands which action is compliant, safe, and commercially viable within a specific environment and organizational guardrails. 

 In life sciences, autonomous manufacturing coordinates processes from design-to-release while strictly adhering to compliance-critical quality and compliance criteria. 

 In energy and natural resources, agents go beyond detecting maintenance alerts to dynamically schedule crews, stage spare parts, and rebalance operations. 

 In engineer-to-order manufacturing, systems orchestrate complex quotations, adapt production schedules, and accelerate new product introductions. 

 Deep industry context is what makes these outcomes trustworthy. 

 Building intelligence that compounds 

 SAP’s Industry AI portfolio is focused across seven core domains: Autonomous Asset Management, Autonomous Commodity Management, Autonomous Adaptive Production, Autonomous Regulated Manufacturing, Autonomous Revenue Growth Management, Autonomous Unified Commerce, and Autonomous Project Delivery. 

 While the use cases differ, the principle is the same: sustainable value comes from end-to-end value streams, not optimizing functional silos. 

 “Business performance depends on how quickly a company can respond when conditions change,” said Andre Bechtold, president of SAP Industries & Experiences and chief revenue officer of Industry AI at SAP. “By applying SAP’s industry knowledge across connected processes, Industry AI helps customers act earlier, limit disruption, and keep operations on track.” 

 The measure that matters 

 Coming out of SAP Connect in 2026 , one message from our customer discussions was unmistakable: the ambition across sectors is to move past fragmented experimentation and embed agentic intelligence directly into mission-critical workflows. 

 Our initial wave of early adopter customers has proven the compounding power of this model: Customer friction points sharpen our agentic solutions, stronger agentic solutions strengthen standard, and stronger standards accelerate the time to value the next customer can achieve. 

 The future of enterprise AI will not be decided by who launches the most agents. It will be decided by who can bring intelligence into the decisions and workflows where business value is created every day. 

 When AI understands the industry, operates within trusted boundaries, and learns alongside human experts, autonomy stops being an abstract vision. It becomes a better way to run the business. 

 For a complete overview of the Industry AI innovations and product announcements unveiled at SAP Connect in 2026, see the SAP Connect Innovation News Guide and related SAP News coverage . 

 Dominik Metzger is president and global head of Industry AI at SAP.

title: SAP PM: як не допустити, щоб поламане обладнання зупинило бізнес
author: Volodymyr
text:
SAP PM: як не допустити, щоб поламане обладнання зупинило бізнес

 Більшість компаній досі в режимі «зламалося → полагодили».
